title: Find Pivot Index
description: Brute force to optimized: resumming both sides at every index versus a running left sum with an algebraically derived right sum.

blocks.text: Given an array of integers nums, find the pivot index: the index where the sum of every element strictly to its left equals the sum of every element strictly to its right. If no such index exists, return -1. If multiple pivot indices exist, return the leftmost one.

blocks.caption: The right side is always derivable as total minus the running left sum minus the current element

blocks.text: Given an array of integers nums, find the pivot index: the index where the sum of every element strictly to its left equals the sum of every element strictly to its right. If no such index exists, return -1. If multiple pivot indices exist, return the leftmost one.

blocks.title: Analogy: Balancing a Seesaw at the Perfect Point
blocks.text: Like sliding a fulcrum along a seesaw loaded with weights at fixed positions, searching for the exact point where the total weight sitting on the left side exactly balances the total weight sitting on the right.

blocks.caption: Slide the balance point until the weight on each side matches exactly

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["At index 3 (value 6): left sum = 1+7+3 = 11, right sum = 5+6 = 11","both sides equal","The elements strictly before index 3 sum to 11, and the elements strictly after index 3 also sum to 11, an exact balance"],["Answer","3","Index 3 is the pivot, and it happens to be the only, and therefore leftmost, valid one"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["No index balances: index 0 gives left 0, right 5; index 1 gives left 1, right 3; index 2 gives left 3, right 0","none match","Every candidate index produces unequal left and right sums"],["Answer","-1","No pivot index exists in this array"]]}

blocks.text: At index 0, the left sum is 0 (nothing exists to the left), and the right sum is 1 + (-1) = 0, so both sides balance trivially, giving pivot index 0.

Before summing both sides independently at every index, notice a simple but powerful identity: the left sum, the current element, and the right sum together always account for every element in the array exactly once, so they must always add up to the same fixed total.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: leftSum(i) plus nums[i] plus rightSum(i) always equals the total sum of the array, since together they cover every element exactly once, regardless of which index i is being considered.

Observation 2: This means rightSum(i) can always be recovered as total minus leftSum(i) minus nums[i], without ever needing to separately scan or track the right portion at all.

Observation 3: leftSum(i) itself can be built incrementally while scanning left to right, since leftSum(i) is just leftSum(i-1) plus nums[i-1], the same running-total idea as a plain prefix sum.

Observation 4: So a single left-to-right pass, maintaining only the running leftSum and the once-computed total, is enough to test every index's balance condition using O(1) work per index, since rightSum is always immediately derivable rather than requiring its own scan.

Whenever a problem needs both a left-side and a right-side aggregate for every position, check whether left plus current plus right always equals a known total; if so, only one running side needs to be tracked, the other is always the total minus what is already known.

This total-minus-known trick is the same insight behind computing a suffix aggregate implicitly instead of building a whole separate structure for it, whenever the total is already known or cheap to compute once.
For every candidate index, separately sum every element to its left and every element to its right, and compare the two sums directly.

items: For each index i, sum every element from index 0 up to, but not including, i for the left sum.
Sum every element from index i plus 1 to the end for the right sum.
If they are equal, i is a pivot index; return the first one found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The left sum stops right before index i, since the pivot condition explicitly excludes the pivot element itself from either side.
The right sum starts at i plus 1, similarly excluding the pivot element itself, since it belongs to neither the left nor the right side by definition.
The function returns the first index found satisfying the balance condition, directly matching the requirement to return the leftmost pivot index, without needing to search further once one is found.

blocks.text: Every candidate index's true left and right sums are directly computed and compared, so the correct leftmost pivot index is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each index re-sums up to n elements across both sides.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the recomputation cost itself.

Limitation: leftSum(i) and rightSum(i) can both be derived from information already known or cheap to maintain, the total sum of the array and a single running left sum, without ever re-scanning either side from scratch.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force treats the left and right sums at every index as two entirely fresh calculations, but both are tightly constrained by one simple fact: together with the element at that index, they must always add up to the same fixed total sum of the array. That constraint means the right sum was never actually independent information at all, it was always fully determined the moment the left sum and the current element were known. Maintaining just one running quantity, the left sum, incrementally as the array is scanned, and deriving the right sum algebraically at each step, replaces two separate O(n) scans per index with two O(1) operations per index, a single subtraction and a single addition.

Compute the total sum of the array once, up front. Then scan left to right, maintaining a running leftSum. At each index, the right sum is simply total minus leftSum minus the current element, so both sides of the balance check are available without a second scan. If they match, that index is the pivot.
Maintain a running left sum while scanning once, deriving the right sum algebraically at every index.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to find the total, one pass to check every index.
Space: O(1) extra.

Since leftSum(i) plus nums[i] plus rightSum(i) always equals the fixed total sum of the array, rightSum(i) is always exactly total minus leftSum(i) minus nums[i], a direct algebraic consequence that holds at every index without needing to verify it separately. Because leftSum only ever grows by exactly one element per step, and always represents the true sum of everything strictly before the current index at the moment it is checked, the derived rightSum is always correct too.

items: total is computed once, in a single pass, before the main scanning loop begins.

leftSum starts at 0, correctly representing the empty left side for index 0, and is only updated after checking the current index, so it always reflects the sum strictly before the current position when the check happens.
The balance check is evaluated fresh at every index, immediately returning that index the moment it succeeds, guaranteeing the leftmost valid pivot is found first.
leftSum is only incremented after the check for the current index, correctly preparing it to represent the left sum for the next index in the following iteration.

blocks.text: This problem rewards spotting a simple algebraic identity, left plus current plus right equals a fixed total, that eliminates the need to track two related quantities independently when tracking just one, plus the known total, is always enough.

items: Forgetting to exclude nums[i] itself from both the left and right sums, since the pivot condition explicitly compares only the strictly-left and strictly-right portions, not including the pivot element.
Updating leftSum before checking the current index's balance condition, instead of after, which would incorrectly include the current element in its own left sum.
Returning the last balancing index found instead of the first, when the problem specifically requires the leftmost pivot index.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A pivot at index 0","Correctly handled since leftSum starts at 0, matching the definition of an empty left side"],["A pivot at the last index","Correctly handled since the derived right sum naturally evaluates to 0 there, as total minus leftSum minus nums[i] leaves nothing over"]]}

items: Explicitly state the identity leftSum plus nums[i] plus rightSum equals the total sum before writing any code, since deriving the optimized approach directly from that one equation is the entire insight.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Compare a left-side aggregate to a right-side aggregate at every position" points toward checking whether left plus current plus right always equals a fixed total; if so, track only one side, since the other is always derivable by subtraction.

items: How would this change if the pivot condition used products instead of sums? The same total-minus-known trick still works using a running left product and a total product, as long as zero values are handled carefully, since a zero would otherwise break the division needed to derive the right side.

What if the array could be updated between pivot-index queries? A plain running sum breaks down under updates; a Fenwick tree or segment tree would let both range sums and pivot-style queries be answered efficiently after updates.

How would you find all pivot indices, not just the leftmost? Continue the same single scan without returning early, collecting every index where the balance condition holds instead of stopping at the first.
Same "total minus known equals unknown" trick as computing a suffix aggregate implicitly from a running prefix total and the overall total, without building a separate suffix array.
Same single running accumulator technique as Running Sum of 1d Array, just paired here with an equality check derived from the total.
Same "exploit an identity to avoid tracking two related quantities separately" insight used in Product of Array Except Self, which similarly derives one side from information already available.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (running leftSum, derived rightSum): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Total-sum-derived right side, combined with an incrementally maintained running left sum
Core Idea: Since leftSum plus nums[i] plus rightSum always equals the fixed total, only leftSum needs to be tracked; rightSum is always total minus leftSum minus nums[i]
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Whenever left plus current plus right sums to a known fixed total, only one side needs active tracking; the other is always recoverable by subtraction
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: rightSum is never scanned, it is always total minus leftSum minus nums[i]
